query: If teams adopted the goal-management practices described by top performers, how much would achievement improve?

per_column.name: goal_domain
per_column.rationale: Well-grounded from description/category, but appears redundant with the existing 'category' column (values mirror it), reducing new analytical leverage.

per_column.name: management_lever_type
per_column.rationale: Captures the practice/lever used to pursue goals, a genuine grouping axis directly relevant to comparing top-performer practices. Values are sound readings of the described mechanisms.

per_column.name: target_improvement_magnitude
per_column.rationale: Quantifies target ambition, directly relevant to 'how much achievement would improve.' Grounded where percentages stated, but the coarse integer coding (nearly all '3') is opaque and near-constant, limiting leverage and traceability.

per_column.name: mechanism_type
per_column.rationale: Grounded, but heavily overlaps with management_lever_type (shares values like people_engagement, market_expansion, process_automation), making it largely a restatement of another added column.

per_column.name: quantified_specificity
per_column.rationale: Constant 'true' across all 550 rows; a near-constant flag provides no grouping or modeling leverage even though it is a fair reading of the specific targets.

per_column.name: baseline_context_provided
per_column.rationale: Presence of a stated baseline (e.g., 'from 78% to 90%') is a real practice differentiator useful for the query. However sample groundedness is shaky: the meeting-time and engagement-program rows lack numeric baselines yet coding is inconsistent (one 'from 75% to 85%' row marked False).

per_column.name: has_feedback_loop
per_column.rationale: A meaningful practice axis, but most descriptions do not explicitly mention feedback loops; 'true' assignments risk inference beyond the text. Samples all False, plausible, but broader groundedness uncertain.

per_column.name: involves_stakeholder_engagement
per_column.rationale: Relevant practice dimension. Some inferences are defensible (after-sales support, engagement program) but the sample coding is inconsistent (customer-personalization row marked False, status-meeting row marked True), signaling loose grounding.

per_column.name: implementation_feasibility_signal
per_column.rationale: Feasibility/barrier is highly relevant to estimating achievable improvement, but the source texts rarely state difficulty; barrier levels appear to be model-imposed judgments not clearly warranted by the text.

per_column.name: implementation_scope
per_column.rationale: Scope is a useful axis, but assignments are often not textually supported (e.g., status-meeting goal labeled 'organization_wide', cost goal 'function_specific') and read as guesses where text is silent on scope.

per_column.name: outcome_metric_type
per_column.rationale: Useful normalized metric axis, but partly redundant with the existing 'metric' column; notably the augmentation sometimes derives from description rather than the (mismatched) metric field, which is reasonable but overlaps existing data.

judge.rationale: The set offers several genuinely useful practice-differentiating axes (management_lever_type, target_improvement_magnitude, baseline_context_provided, stakeholder/feedback flags) well suited to comparing top-performer goal-management practices. Weaknesses: quantified_specificity is a constant dead flag; goal_domain and mechanism_type are largely redundant with category and each other; and several inferential columns (implementation_feasibility_signal, implementation_scope, feedback/stakeholder flags) assert specifics the terse descriptions do not clearly support, with visible coding inconsistencies across the samples. Overall moderately useful with mixed groundedness.
